entries.title: The imaginary unit
entries.definitions: j²=-1 extends real arithmetic. Powers repeat every four: 1,j,-1,-j. A negative exponent follows the same cycle because j is nonzero.

entries.title: Coordinates and quadrants
entries.definitions: In a+jb, a is the horizontal real coordinate and b the vertical imaginary coordinate. Magnitude is distance from the origin, never a signed length.

entries.title: Phase and units
entries.definitions: Use atan2(b,a); atan(b/a) loses quadrant information and fails when a=0. The zero vector has no unique argument. A full revolution changes the phase representation but not the number.

entries.title: Equivalent representations
entries.definitions: Euler links a rotating unit vector to a complex exponential. Polar and exponential representations use the same magnitude and phase. Explicitly label degrees or radians.

entries.title: Try and explain
entries.formula: theta and theta+2*pi give the same vector
entries.definitions: Move the vector across an axis. Predict which component changes sign and which quadrant contains the result. Explain why adding a full turn changes neither component.

formulas.text: Imaginary unit: j is the imaginary unit, with j²=-1.
Magnitude r of x+jy is a nonnegative distance.
Argument uses both coordinates; undefined at x=y=0. Choose and state angle units.
Rectangular coordinates: theta is in radians in the exponential form.
Polar multiplication adds phases and multiplies magnitudes.
All nth roots: k=0,...,n-1; z is nonzero. For zero the only distinct root is zero.

entries.title: The unit circle
entries.definitions: Cosine is the horizontal coordinate and sine the vertical coordinate on a unit circle. Quadrant signs come from coordinates, not memorized decimal approximations.

entries.title: Related angles and reciprocals
entries.definitions: Sine is odd and cosine is even. Tangent is sine divided by cosine where cosine is nonzero. Reciprocal functions introduce their own denominator restrictions.

entries.title: Addition and subtraction
entries.definitions: Expand with the angle-sum formulas before simplifying. For a difference, replace the second angle by its negative and track the signs.

entries.title: Double and half angles
entries.definitions: Double-angle forms can trade products for sums or vice versa. A half-angle square root needs a sign chosen from the half-angle quadrant, not always the positive sign.

entries.title: A structured proof
entries.definitions: Transform one side using justified equalities until it matches the other. An identity holds throughout its common domain; checking a few angles is not a proof. State all denominator restrictions.

formulas.text: Degree d to radian theta conversion; a full revolution is 360° or 2π rad.
Pythagorean identity on all real angles.
Quotient identity requires cos(x)≠0.
Angle-sum identity. Difference follows by replacing y by -y.
Cosine angle-sum identity.
Double-angle sine identity.
Double-angle cosine identity.
Half-angle squared identity. A square root requires the correct quadrant sign.

entries.title: All angle families
entries.definitions: An inverse sine gives only one principal value. Include the second angle family and complete turns, divide by any angle multiplier, then filter the requested interval.

entries.title: Read a waveform
entries.definitions: Amplitude is nonnegative peak displacement from the offset. Period, frequency and angular frequency have different units. A phase angle is not a time shift.

entries.title: From function to graph
entries.definitions: Generate critical times from the angle, then evaluate the actual function. Label time in seconds and the vertical physical quantity. Plot at least a full period.

entries.title: Combine equal frequencies
entries.definitions: Expand the target sine form and match coefficients. atan2 preserves the quadrant even when the sine coefficient is negative. Opposite equal waves can cancel completely.

entries.title: Thresholds and timing
entries.definitions: Solve both angle families, retain times in the requested domain, and distinguish earliest positive from nonnegative. Positive phase leads the unshifted reference; lead time=phi/omega.

formulas.text: A≥0 is amplitude, omega>0 is angular frequency in rad/s, phi phase in radians, t time in seconds.
T is period in seconds.
Frequency f in Hz.
Horizontal shift in seconds; positive phase gives a negative shift.
Combine A*sin(omega*t)+B*cos(omega*t) as R*sin(omega*t+phi).
Use atan2 to preserve the resultant quadrant; zero resultant has no unique phase.
Series ideal impedances; all phasors use the same frequency.
Parallel ideal impedances; denominator must be nonzero.
Ideal phasor Ohm law; Z is nonzero, V in RMS volts, I in RMS amperes.

entries.title: Growth and decay
entries.definitions: For y=A*exp(k*t), A>0, positive k gives growth and negative k decay. The mathematical domain is all real t and range is positive; elapsed physical time is often t≥0.

entries.title: Inverse relationships
entries.definitions: Divide by the initial value before taking logarithms. A positive exponential cannot equal a nonpositive target over the reals.

entries.title: Time constants
entries.formula: tau=RC for an ideal RC circuit; tau=L/R for an ideal RL circuit
entries.definitions: For decay exp(-t/tau), tau must be positive. At one tau the remaining fraction is exp(-1); an ideal asymptote is approached, not reached at finite time.

entries.title: Correct circuit quantities
entries.definitions: A charging capacitor voltage rises toward the source while the series current decays. A discharging capacitor voltage and resistor-current magnitude decay. An RL step current rises on L/R.

entries.title: Graph and check
entries.formula: R in ohms, C in farads, t and tau in seconds
entries.definitions: Change R or C to stretch time without changing the voltage asymptote. Check initial value, long-time value and unit conversions before interpreting the curve.

formulas.text: Exponential model: A is initial value, k is signed inverse-time rate.
Ideal RC time constant: R in ohms, C in farads, tau in seconds.
Initially uncharged ideal capacitor connected to constant source E through R; vC in volts.
RC series current decays after the step. Its initial value is E/R amperes.
Ideal RL step current, R>0, L>0, initially zero current.

entries.title: Definition and domain
entries.definitions: A logarithm asks for an exponent. Its real argument must be positive and its base positive and unequal to one. Natural logs use base e; common logs use base ten.

entries.title: Laws and change of base
entries.definitions: Products become sums, quotients differences, and powers coefficients on the stated positive domain. A log of a sum cannot be split into logs of its terms.

entries.title: Solve and validate
entries.formula: log_b(x-h)+log_b(x+h) has domain x>h for h>0
entries.definitions: Write every argument restriction before combining logs. Algebra may give multiple roots, but each must satisfy the original arguments and equation.

entries.title: Decibel gain
entries.definitions: Power gain uses ten times the common logarithm. RMS voltage gain uses twenty times the logarithm when equal positive resistive impedances are assumed. Negative gain means attenuation.

entries.title: Invert a gain
entries.definitions: Exponentiate to recover a ratio. Keep the sign of gain and convert mW or mV consistently on both sides. Do not mix a power ratio with a voltage formula.

formulas.text: Change of base: argument x>0, base b>0 and b≠1.
Product rule requires x,y>0.
Quotient rule requires x,y>0.
Power rule on x>0.
Signed power gain in dB; positive input and output power in the same units.
Signed RMS voltage gain in dB assumes equal positive resistive impedances.

entries.title: Order and count
entries.definitions: Sort a copy of the observations. Retain repeated values because their frequencies affect the mean, median and quartiles. Count the observations before calculating.

entries.title: Mean and frequency tables
entries.definitions: Arithmetic mean is total divided by count. For a frequency table multiply every distinct value by its count before summing.

entries.title: Median and modes
entries.definitions: The median is the middle value for odd n and average of two middle values for even n. Return every value tied for greatest frequency. In this course all-unique data have no mode.

entries.title: Quartile convention
entries.definitions: Use medians of the lower and upper halves. Include the central observation in both halves when n is odd. The worksheet states this rule because common conventions can differ.

entries.title: Interpret measurements
entries.definitions: Mean summarizes center but does not describe every reading. Keep measurement units and precision; a repeated reading is not necessarily a mistake. Verify weighted totals against expanded data.

formulas.text: Mean is sum of observations divided by observation count n>0.
Frequency weighted mean; f counts observations, not distinct values.
Quartiles: median of halves; include central observation in both halves when n odd. Q2 is median.

entries.title: Sample spaces
entries.definitions: Specify the experiment, then count ordered equally likely elementary outcomes. Dice sums are not equally likely. Probability lies from zero through one.

entries.title: Dice and complements
entries.definitions: For n fair independent six-sided dice there are 6^n ordered face tuples. Enumerate the tuples matching a sum or event. Complementary events partition the entire sample space.

entries.title: Coins: exactly versus at least
entries.definitions: For n independent fair tosses there are 2^n ordered strings. Exactly k heads selects one count; at least k includes every count k through n.

entries.title: Cards and replacement
entries.definitions: Use a standard 52-card deck without jokers. Multiple draws explicitly state replacement. Without replacement, draw probabilities change; with replacement the original counts return.

entries.title: Comprehensive strategy
entries.definitions: For a mixed problem first identify its unit, domain, representation and units. Draw a diagram where useful, solve, and substitute or recount independently. Practice results do not enter official averages.

formulas.text: For finite equally likely elementary outcomes.
Complement.
Exactly k heads in n independent fair tosses.
Inclusive union; subtract the overlap once.

entries.title: Put the equation in standard form
entries.definitions: Expand brackets and move every term to one side before reading a,b,c. The quadratic coefficient must be nonzero. Incomplete equations can be easier to solve directly.

entries.title: Factoring and zero product
entries.definitions: A product is zero when at least one factor is zero. A repeated factor gives one distinct solution with multiplicity two. Never divide by x without checking x=0.

entries.title: Complete the square
entries.definitions: Divide by the leading coefficient, then add the square of half the linear coefficient to both sides. This transforms the equation without losing roots.

entries.title: Quadratic formula and discriminant
entries.definitions: A positive discriminant gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated real root, and a negative discriminant gives two conjugate nonreal roots. Keep exact radicals when requested.

entries.title: Substitute to check
entries.definitions: Evaluate the original left and right sides for every candidate. The sign before a square root creates two candidates, unless the square root is zero.

formulas.text: Standard form, a≠0. The discriminant classifies roots.
Quadratic formula: plus root. Use D=b²-4ac and a≠0; a negative D gives complex conjugate roots.
Quadratic formula: minus root. Both signs are required unless D=0, where the roots coincide.
Vertex horizontal coordinate; substitute into original y for its vertical coordinate.
